blocks.text: Fig. 51(a) tracks DreamDojo rollout success and native RoboLab success at twelve policy checkpoints, including SFT. Native RoboLab success reaches 71% in evaluations of 100 episodes per policy. The separate final evaluation uses 5,000 episodes per policy and shows an increase from 51.32% to 70.88%. DreamDojo success is measured by the learned reward on training rollouts, whereas RoboLab evaluation uses native task outcomes. Because the sampling procedures and horizons differ, these curves track learning within each setting rather than measure simulator calibration.

blocks.text: Fig. 51(b) compares eleven matched collection budgets through 67,584 trajectories. The larger combined batch/group configuration has higher native RoboLab success at ten budgets, and its success rate is 11.1 percentage points higher on average across the eleven budgets. At the final budget, success is 71% versus 54%, a 17-point difference. At 24,576 trajectories, the rates are 68% and 47%, respectively.

blocks.text: These single-run results favor the larger combined recipe. They also differ in optimization and reset layout: at the final budget, the smaller recipe has made 528 optimizer updates and the larger one 176. Late continuation of the smaller recipe additionally removed a numerical lower log-ratio bound. These differences limit attribution to either size parameter, and one run per configuration does not establish stability across independent runs.

blocks.text: Discussion. These results demonstrate policy improvement using experience generated by a world model adapted to an initial policy’s rollouts. GR00T 2 learns in this environment and is evaluated in RoboLab and on real-world robots. The current pipeline still requires task-rollout collection and task-specific world-model adaptation. Reusing the learned environment across new tasks and repeating the full world-model and policy improvement cycle remain directions for future work.
blocks.section: F.5. Reinforcement Learning with Neural Simulation

blocks.text: Our experiments focus on individual manipulation skills that serve as building blocks for more complex robot behavior. These skills can be integrated into agentic execution (Sec. G.1), where high-level orchestration, progress monitoring, and recovery coordinate actions across longer task horizons. RL-based adaptation and agentic execution therefore provide complementary mechanisms for improving robot reliability, from finegrained physical interactions to long-horizon task completion.
blocks.section: F.5. Reinforcement Learning with Neural Simulation

blocks.text: Our longer-term goal is to develop scalable post-training methods that enable world-action models to improve consistently through real-world experience, extending their capabilities to increasingly challenging manipulation tasks.
blocks.section: F.5. Reinforcement Learning with Neural Simulation

blocks.text: G. Agentic GR00T 2
blocks.section: G. Agentic GR00T 2

blocks.text: Pretraining and post-training equip GR00T 2 with increasingly capable manipulation skills, but robust longhorizon execution requires more than a strong underlying policy. Complex tasks involve multiple stages, task-level decisions, and unexpected failures that are difficult to resolve through continuous policy execution alone. Language instructions can also leave important aspects of task intent underspecified, such as which object to manipulate or where to place it.
blocks.section: G. Agentic GR00T 2

blocks.text: We explore two complementary approaches to agentic manipulation. First, agentic skill composition and recovery integrates GR00T 2 with CaP, enabling higher-level agents to compose manipulation skills, monitor execution, and recover from unexpected failures (Sec. G.1). Second, steerable world-action generation exposes GR00T 2’s learned capabilities through the WAM API, allowing agents to guide and compose robot behaviors using visual targets (Sec. G.2). Together, these approaches enable higher-level reasoning agents to leverage GR00T 2 for complex, long-horizon manipulation.
blocks.section: G. Agentic GR00T 2

blocks.text: G.1. Agentic Skill Composition and Recovery with Code-as-Policy
blocks.section: G.1. Agentic Skill Composition and Recovery with Code-as-Policy

blocks.text: Even after post-training, long-horizon manipulation remains vulnerable to compounding errors and unforeseen states (Ross et al., 2011). We introduce an agentic execution framework in which a frontier multimodal coding agent serves as System 2 (S2), composing GR00T 2 with CaP tools while monitoring task progress and recovering from failures. The agent verifies each intervention before resuming execution, without requiring GR00T 2 to learn every contingency.
blocks.section: G.1. Agentic Skill Composition and Recovery with Code-as-Policy

blocks.text: The same framework supports complementary execution strategies. In simulation, we use ASPIRE (Lu et al., 2026) to discover task-level programs that call GR00T 2 as a manipulation tool, and each task runs either its program or GR00T 2 alone as the default executor, whichever succeeds more often on development seeds. On physical robots, where GR00T 2 is already capable of handling most manipulation, it remains the default controller. In both settings, S2 provides monitoring and CaP-based recovery. The key distinction is what executes between interventions.
blocks.section: G.1. Agentic Skill Composition and Recovery with Code-as-Policy

blocks.text: Agentic Runtime Architecture. The runtime exposes GR00T 2 execution, robot observations, and CaP primitives through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). S2 uses these tools in an observe-reason-act-verify loop (Fig. 6).
blocks.section: G.1. Agentic Skill Composition and Recovery with Code-as-Policy

blocks.text: The wam_act tool executes GR00T 2 with a task prompt and returns execution feedback. The agent can access camera observations and robot state through dedicated observation tools and adjust GR00T 2’s language prompt during execution if needed. The stop_wam tool terminates GR00T 2 execution when a recovery action requires control. CaP action primitives issue end-effector and gripper commands through inverse kinematics and motion planning, while observation primitives use vision foundation models for information such as object localization and pose estimation. CaP programs compose these primitives into executable skills that can be added at test time without retraining GR00T 2. A single control worker coordinates actuation so that GR00T 2 and CaP do not issue conflicting robot commands.
blocks.section: G.1. Agentic Skill Composition and Recovery with Code-as-Policy

blocks.text: The agent receives an operating guide (AGENTS.md), skill documentation, and task context describing stages, success criteria, and known failure modes. It checks observations and tool feedback for stalled progress or errors, then invokes a recovery action when needed. Recovery may involve regrasping a dropped part, reorienting a component, or returning the robot to a valid configuration before execution resumes.
blocks.section: G.1. Agentic Skill Composition and Recovery with Code-as-Policy

blocks.text: Program and Skill Acquisition. ASPIRE learns the executable behaviors used alongside GR00T 2, but the scope differs by setting. In simulation, it discovers task-level CaP programs that compose GR00T 2 calls with perception, geometric reasoning, and manipulation primitives. During online execution, S2 may reuse or adapt code from these programs for recovery. On physical robots, ASPIRE instead acquires targeted CaP skills, either through direct robot interaction or through CaP sim-to-real transfer, in which skills are learned in simulation and adapted to real-world conditions (Sec. J.2.4).
blocks.section: G.1. Agentic Skill Composition and Recovery with Code-as-Policy

blocks.text: Simulation Evaluation. We evaluate on RoboCasa365 (Nasiriany et al., 2026) and RoboDojo (Chen et al., 2026a) using four configurations: SFT, SFT + RL, SFT + Agent, and SFT + RL + Agent. For agentic execution, ASPIRE discovers programs using 15 development seeds per task. On 30 development seeds, including those 15, we then run each task’s program and GR00T 2 alone, and make whichever succeeds more often the task’s default executor, keeping the program on ties. With the SFT checkpoint, this selects GR00T 2 for 23 of the 50 RoboCasa365 tasks and 12 of the 54 RoboDojo task configurations. S2 starts every episode with the default executor, monitors it, and invokes online CaP recovery when needed. We test on 50 held-out seeds per task on both benchmarks (25 each for the standard and randomized variants of RoboDojo’s generalization tasks), disjoint from the development seeds.
blocks.section: G.1. Agentic Skill Composition and Recovery with Code-as-Policy

blocks.text: With SFT alone, GR00T 2 achieves the highest success rate of any non-agentic policy on both the RoboCasa365 and RoboDojo leaderboards (Sec. J.3 and Tab. 19). Memory- and reasoning-based tasks and high-precision manipulation still leave room for improvement.
blocks.section: G.1. Agentic Skill Composition and Recovery with Code-as-Policy

blocks.text: RL post-training with AutoRL (Sec. F.2) mainly improves precision, raising RoboDojo Precision success from 40.5% to 53.7%, and lifts average success from 67.2% to 72.4% on RoboCasa365 and from 35.2% to 40.8% on RoboDojo layout bank 0 (Tab. 19). Agentic execution helps most on memory- and reasoning-focused tasks: ASPIRE programs and S2 raise success on RoboCasa365 Composite-Unseen tasks from 38.2% to 69.5% and on RoboDojo Memory tasks from 36.0% to 93.7%. Overall, it brings average success to 81.8% on RoboCasa365 and 72.3% on RoboDojo, and combining it with RL gives the best results on both benchmarks. Compared with the top entries of both public leaderboards, including agentic submissions, SFT + RL + Agent ranks first on RoboCasa365 (88.0% vs. 85.6% for HexaShell 1.5) and on RoboDojo, where we evaluate layout bank 0 only (75.8% vs. 68.9% for Q0-Preview) (Tab. 19).
blocks.section: G.1. Agentic Skill Composition and Recovery with Code-as-Policy

blocks.text: Table 20: Episode outcomes by whether S2 intervenes (SFT + Agent). Each cell gives the number of episodes and how many of them succeed, over all episodes of the SFT + Agent runs (2,093 on RoboDojo and 2,500 on RoboCasa365).
blocks.section: G.1. Agentic Skill Composition and Recovery with Code-as-Policy

blocks.text: To characterize online recovery in the SFT + Agent setting, we split episodes by whether S2 intervened (Tab. 20). S2 rarely lets a failure through: of the episodes it leaves untouched, only 29 of 1,320 fail on RoboDojo and 20 of 1,512 on RoboCasa365. Of the episodes it intervenes in, 24% succeed on RoboDojo (188 of 773) and 56% on RoboCasa365 (553 of 988). Fig. 53 shows one rescue and one failed recovery.
blocks.section: G.1. Agentic Skill Composition and Recovery with Code-as-Policy

blocks.text: A manual review of failed SFT + Agent episodes on both benchmarks (Fig. 54) shows that most failures fall into two groups: the recovery requires manipulation too precise for S2 to perform with motion-planning tools (38% on RoboCasa365, 39% on RoboDojo), or the episode reaches a state that can no longer be recovered, such as an object on the floor or too little time left (24% and 38%). Most of the rest look complete but do not satisfy the benchmark’s success check.
blocks.section: G.1. Agentic Skill Composition and Recovery with Code-as-Policy

blocks.text: Real-World Long-Horizon Manipulation. We evaluate agentic execution with GR00T 2 as the default controller on multi-stage assembly and repeated precision insertion, examining how CaP recovery complements policy post-training.
blocks.section: G.1. Agentic Skill Composition and Recovery with Code-as-Policy

blocks.text: Multi-stage assembly. We consider Toy Plane, Toy Tractor, and Hot Wheels assembly (Fig. 55). To stress-test robustness, each episode begins by dumping parts onto the table, producing clutter and varied object poses. The robot must assemble the parts in order, use a toy drill, and recover from execution errors. We compare SFT, SFT + DAgger (Ross et al., 2011), and SFT + DAgger + Agent.
blocks.section: G.1. Agentic Skill Composition and Recovery with Code-as-Policy

blocks.text: The Toy Plane task assembles a fuselage, two wings, and two screws using a toy drill. It requires seating and fastening the bottom wing, turning the airplane over, and fastening the top wing, with bimanual handovers and accurate screw-hole alignment. Success requires both wings fastened and the drill set down. The Toy Tractor task mounts and fastens two small front wheels and two large rear wheels, turning the body over between sides and returning it upright at the end. The Hot Wheels task mounts the correct front and rear wheels and installs a correctly oriented hood, fastening the components with a drill.
blocks.section: G.1. Agentic Skill Composition and Recovery with Code-as-Policy

blocks.text: Fig. 7a reports the results. DAgger improves Toy Plane Assembly, Toy Tractor Assembly, and Hot Wheels Assembly success from 69%, 51%, and 23% to 84%, 71%, and 78%, respectively. Adding agentic execution further increases success to 98%, 97%, and 97%. This improvement reflects the ability of S2 to detect and repair local execution failures while preserving GR00T 2’s learned manipulation capabilities. Because every trial starts from parts dumped at random, these success rates measure robustness to unseen starting configurations and are not directly comparable with the post-training benchmark (Tab. 1a), whose trials start from arranged layouts. For Hot Wheels Assembly, for example, the benchmark reports 85% success from its fixed layout.
blocks.section: G.1. Agentic Skill Composition and Recovery with Code-as-Policy
